c.tagline: Ireland's rebel city — a foodie harbour town of pubs, bells and Georgian charm.

taxi.fareNote: There is no private ride-share in Ireland — Uber operates only as a licensed-taxi dispatcher. Hail on the street, use a rank, or book via the FreeNow app; metered fares are set by national regulation.

emergency.note: 112 (EU-wide) and 999 both connect to Garda (police), ambulance, fire, and coast guard.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.Shandon: Shandon Bells and St Anne's Church, Cork

avoid.reason: Usual late-night pub-crowd awareness around St Patrick's Street and Oliver Plunkett Street at weekend closing time.

hood_desc: The compact island city centre between the two channels of the River Lee, home to St Patrick's Street, the covered English Market, Grand Parade and the main shops; the walkable base where most first-timers stay.

The historic north-side hill district crowned by the Shandon Bells and St Anne's Church, with the old Butter Exchange, Firkin Crane and steep lanes of pastel houses; steeped in sightseeing and local character.

The revived MacCurtain Street strip on the near north bank, Cork's 'Victorian Quarter' of independent restaurants, cocktail bars, music venues and boutique hotels; the heart of the city's going-out scene.

A leafy southside suburb around Douglas Village and its shopping centres, with quiet residential streets and easy access to the coast road; popular with families and longer-stay visitors wanting calm.
The elegant tree-lined avenue running west past University College Cork, Fitzgerald Park and the Cork Public Museum, dotted with Georgian guesthouses; a genteel, green base near the university.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 6:00 AM to 11:30 PM, with limited NiteLink services on weekends; commuter trains run from early morning to late evening.
transit.note: Cork has no metro or tram; getting around means Bus Éireann city buses and the Cork commuter rail lines out of Kent Station, plus a very walkable compact centre.
transit.pay: Tap on with a Leap Card or contactless bank card; cash is accepted on buses (exact fare preferred). Leap Cards give cheaper capped fares.

tip.r: Not expected; rounding up the bill or leaving ~10% for good table service in restaurants is appreciated.

food.name: Cork buttered eggs
food.desc: A near-extinct Cork trick: warm eggs rolled in butter so it seals the shell, keeping them fresh and giving the yolk a rich, faintly creamy taste.

places.name: The English Market egg stalls
places.note: One of the last places in Ireland still selling buttered eggs, made the old way.

places.name: Farmgate Cafe
places.note: Cooks market produce a few metres from where it is sold; award-winning breakfasts.

places.name: On the Pig's Back
places.note: Long-established deli counter for buttered eggs, local cheese and charcuterie.

food.name: Tripe and drisheen
food.desc: Cork's most hardcore native dish: honeycomb tripe simmered in milk with drisheen, a soft sheep's-blood pudding, usually with white pepper.

places.name: O'Reilly's Tripe and Drisheen
places.note: The last dedicated tripe and drisheen stall in Ireland, a genuine Cork institution.

places.name: Farmgate Cafe
places.note: Serves the classic tripe and drisheen plate for anyone who wants it cooked.

places.name: The English Market butchers' row
places.note: Several butchers still stock drisheen to take away, best asked for early.

food.name: Cork spiced beef
food.desc: Beef cured for weeks with saltpetre, pimento and juniper, then boiled or roasted and sliced thin; a Cork Christmas fixture sold year round.

places.name: Tom Durcan Meats
places.note: The name Corkonians queue at for spiced beef; ships nationwide at Christmas.

places.name: Farmgate Cafe
places.note: Puts market spiced beef straight onto sandwiches and plates upstairs.

places.name: Market Lane
places.note: Busy city-centre restaurant that cooks local suppliers, spiced beef included.

food.name: Blaas and Cork sourdough breads
food.desc: Soft, floury white bread rolls from Ireland's south-east eaten split with butter, alongside Cork's own sourdough and brown soda breads.

places.name: Alternative Bread Company
places.note: Market bakery stall with a long queue for soda bread and sourdough loaves.

places.name: Arbutus Breads
places.note: Cork's best-known artisan bakery; its bread is on most good local menus.

places.name: Nash 19
places.note: Local-supplier cafe where the bread basket is a showcase of Cork bakers.

food.name: West Cork seafood chowder
food.desc: Creamy chowder of smoked haddock, salmon and mussels landed on the west Cork coast, served with brown soda bread and butter.

places.name: The Oyster Tavern
places.note: Old Cork name reopened as a seafood-led bar and restaurant off Patrick Street.

places.name: Electric
places.note: Fish bar upstairs with harbour-fresh seafood and river views.

places.name: Market Lane
places.note: Dependable all-day kitchen using English Market fish and Cork dairy.

food.name: Full Irish with Clonakilty pudding
food.desc: The Cork breakfast plate: rashers, sausage, egg and both black and white Clonakilty pudding, with fried soda bread on the side.

places.name: Farmgate Cafe
places.note: Breakfast built entirely from stalls downstairs; the classic Cork morning.

places.name: Nash 19
places.note: Award-winning local-food cafe with a strong traceable-supplier breakfast.

places.name: The Woodford
places.note: Central pub doing a solid all-day fry when the market cafes are full.

food.name: Murphy's Irish Stout
food.desc: Cork's own dry stout, brewed in Blackpool since 1856 and noticeably softer and sweeter than Dublin's; ordering it here is a local loyalty test.

places.name: The Mutton Lane Inn
places.area: Off Patrick Street, by the English Market
places.note: Candlelit 1787 laneway pub, the classic first pint in Cork.

places.name: Sin E
places.note: Cork's best-loved trad-music pub, with sessions most nights and a proper pour.

places.name: The Oval Bar
places.note: Old-school city-centre bar for a quiet, well-kept stout.

food.name: Barry's Tea
food.desc: Blended in Cork since 1901 and drunk here with fierce loyalty; a strong, malty cup served in every cafe, pub kitchen and market stall in the city.

places.name: Farmgate Cafe
places.note: A pot of tea with brown bread is the standard Cork market break.

places.name: Nash 19
places.note: Local-first cafe where the tea comes with home baking.

places.name: Idaho Cafe
places.note: Tiny long-running city-centre cafe beloved for its baking and cuppa.

landmarks: The English Market
Trading since 1788 beneath vaulted Victorian ceilings, Cork's beloved covered food market overflows with artisan cheeses, spiced beef, and the city's gossip.
St. Fin Barre's Cathedral
William Burges's triple-spired French Gothic masterpiece of 1879 rises on Cork's founding monastic site, guarded by the famous golden Resurrection Angel.
Blarney Castle and the Blarney Stone
A short trip from the city, kissing the legendary stone atop this 15th-century tower house bestows eloquence, with poison gardens and glens below.
Shandon Bells and St. Anne's Church
Climb the pepper-pot tower of 1722, ring the famous bells yourself, and survey Cork's hilly panorama beneath the goldfish weathervane.
Cork City Gaol
A castle-like 19th-century prison on Sunday's Well hill, its restored cells and lifelike figures recount the grim stories of Victorian inmates.
University College Cork and the Glucksman Gallery
A riverside Victorian Gothic quadrangle houses one of Ireland's loveliest campuses, with ogham stones, the Honan Chapel, and an award-winning gallery.
Elizabeth Fort
A 17th-century star-shaped artillery fort off Barrack Street, its ramparts now offer free entry and one of the best skyline views over the city.
Crawford Art Gallery
Cork's national gallery in the 1724 Custom House pairs Greek and Roman cast sculptures with Irish masters from James Barry to Harry Clarke.
St. Patrick's Street and the Grand Parade
Cork's curving main artery, rebuilt after the 1920 Burning of Cork, sweeps past Victorian facades to the riverside where the old city walls once stood.
Fitzgerald Park and Cork Public Museum
The city's graceful riverside park pairs rose gardens and the Sky Garden with a museum of Cork's republican and sporting history, beside Daly's shaky footbridge.

train.note: All trains use Kent Station on Lower Glanmire Road, about 500 m east of the city centre and a 10-minute walk from Patrick Street. Intercity services to Dublin Heuston run roughly hourly and take about 2 hr 40 min, with connections at Mallow for Tralee and Killarney and at Limerick Junction for the west; suburban trains serve Midleton and Cobh. There is no international train from Cork - Ireland's only cross-border service is the Enterprise between Dublin and Belfast, so you change in Dublin. Advance web fares booked a few days ahead are far cheaper than walk-up tickets.

intl.to: Belfast & Derry (UK) - no direct coach; change at Dublin Airport onto the 705X

bus.note: Coaches use Cork Bus Station at Parnell Place off Merchants Quay, five minutes' walk from the centre. Bus Eireann Expressway (https://www.buseireann.ie/) and Aircoach's 704X (https://www.aircoach.ie/) both run to Dublin city and Dublin Airport in 3-3.5 hrs for around 20 euro, and Bus Eireann also serves Limerick, Galway, Waterford and Rosslare Europort for the Welsh and French ferries. No coach runs directly from Cork across a border, so Belfast means changing in Dublin onto Aircoach or Translink, a total of about 6.5 hours; there are no passport checks on the island of Ireland. Fares are cheapest booked online, and Leap cards work on city services.

intl.to: Roscoff (France) - sails from the Cork Ferry Terminal at Ringaskiddy, 15 km southeast of the city on the N28

ferry.note: Ringaskiddy is about 25 minutes from the city by car or Bus Eireann connection, and check-in closes well before departure. The Cork-Roscoff sailing is seasonal rather than year-round, generally running from spring into autumn, and takes roughly 14-15 hours overnight with cabins strongly recommended; the former Cork-Santander service no longer operates, so for northern Spain you use Brittany Ferries' Rosslare-Bilbao route instead. Cars and cabins should be booked months ahead for July and August. Closer to home, the Cross River Ferry between Carrigaloe and Glenbrook runs continuously and saves a long drive around the harbour, and passenger boats serve Cobh and Spike Island.

half.name: Kinsale
half.blurb: A colorful harbor town famed for its gourmet food scene, marina and the star-shaped Charles Fort overlooking the bay.

half.name: Cobh
half.blurb: A hillside port town that was the Titanic's final port of call, with a heritage center on its emigration history.

half.name: Kilkenny
half.blurb: A medieval city dominated by a Norman castle, with a preserved cathedral and cobbled Medieval Mile of laneways.

half.name: Midleton
half.blurb: Home to the Jameson Distillery's original site, where whiskey has been made since the 18th century.

full.name: Killarney and Ring of Kerry
full.blurb: A lakeside town gateway to a scenic coastal driving loop of mountains, cliffs and Killarney National Park.
